name: Ciclopirox shampoo

lead: Ciclopirox shampoo is a medicated antifungal wash used to clear the flaking, redness and itching of seborrheic dermatitis, the inflamed scalp condition that overlaps with dandruff. The payoff is a cleaner, flake-free scalp and hair. It is prescription-only in the US.

Ciclopirox is a hydroxypyridone antifungal active against Malassezia yeasts and described as having anti-inflammatory properties; its mechanism differs from the azoles and is not fully understood. Randomized trials have tested the 1% shampoo against vehicle for scalp seborrheic dermatitis and as an adjunct in childhood tinea capitis. No trial found tested it for hair growth.

paras: People use it as a regular medicated wash, often alternating with or alongside ketoconazole shampoo in hair-loss and scalp-care circles. Flaking typically improves over a few weeks of repeated use.
Systemic absorption from topical use is reported to be low. It is a prescription medicine in the US and Canada; local irritation is the usual concern with medicated shampoos.

angle.text: Ciclopirox shampoo targets the Malassezia yeast behind scalp flaking and redness, leaving a cleaner, flake-free scalp and hair. Several vehicle-controlled trials cover seborrheic dermatitis; none have examined hair growth.

lead: Ciclopirox shampoo is a medicated shampoo containing the synthetic hydroxypyridone antifungal ciclopirox, used mainly to treat seborrheic dermatitis of the scalp, a common inflammatory condition that causes flaking, redness and itching and overlaps with ordinary dandruff.[1][2] Ciclopirox is a broad-spectrum antifungal with reported anti-inflammatory properties and is active against Malassezia yeasts, which are implicated in seborrheic dermatitis.[3][4]

In appearance and hair-loss communities, ciclopirox shampoo is sometimes mentioned as an alternative or companion to ketoconazole shampoo for scalp flaking and, more speculatively, for scalp health in people with hair loss. Published trials have examined it for seborrheic dermatitis and, as an adjunct, for tinea capitis (scalp ringworm) in children; no published trial found in the sources examined tested it as a hair-growth treatment.[5][6]
In the United States, ciclopirox is a prescription-only medicine, according to Wikipedia.[1]
infobox: Topical (shampoo, also nail lacquer and creams)
Prescription-only in the US and Canada; pharmacy medicine (S2) in Australia

paras: The best-documented use is the treatment of seborrheic dermatitis of the scalp, for which 1% ciclopirox shampoo has been tested in several randomized trials.[2][3][7] A 2007 comparison cited by Wikipedia described ciclopirox as an alternative to ketoconazole with similar efficacy and greater subjective symptom relief, possibly because of its anti-inflammatory action.[1]
Ciclopirox shampoo has also been studied as an adjunct to oral griseofulvin in children with tinea capitis.[5][6] Other ciclopirox formulations are used for fungal nail infections.[1]

Wikipedia describes the mechanism of ciclopirox as poorly understood and distinct from the azole antifungals; loss of function of certain catalase and peroxidase enzymes has been implicated, and yeast studies suggest effects on DNA repair, cell division and intracellular transport.[1] Reviews describe it as effective in vitro and in vivo against Malassezia yeasts and as having anti-inflammatory properties.[4] Systemic absorption with prolonged topical use is reported as under 5 percent, with high protein binding.[1]

Several randomized, vehicle-controlled trials have evaluated 1% ciclopirox shampoo in scalp seborrheic dermatitis. A US trial enrolled 499 patients who applied ciclopirox shampoo or vehicle twice weekly for four weeks.[2] A European multicenter trial across 45 centers tested once- or twice-weekly use for four weeks and then followed responders in a 12-week prophylaxis phase.[3] Another trial compared different concentrations of the shampoo against vehicle.[8] An Italian assessor-blinded trial in moderate-to-severe scalp seborrheic dermatitis was published in 2019.[7] Narrative reviews summarize this body of work.[4][9]

In tinea capitis, a randomized double-blind study of 40 children compared selenium sulfide 1% and ciclopirox 1% shampoos as adjuncts to eight weeks of griseofulvin.[5] A registered trial examined selenium sulfide, ketoconazole and ciclopirox shampoos as additional treatments for scalp ringworm.[6]
No published trials found in these sources test ciclopirox shampoo for hair growth in androgenetic alopecia.
Ciclopirox shampoo is a minor topic compared with ketoconazole shampoo in hair-loss communities. Where it appears, participants discuss it as a prescription antifungal option for scalp inflammation.
